newsitem.title: USA: White House says FBI kept Clinton in dark on China.
newsitem.headline: White House says FBI kept Clinton in dark on China.

text.p: The FBI warned White House officials of a suspected Chinese plan to buy U.S. political influence but asked them not to tell higher-ups, leaving President Bill Clinton in the dark, Clinton's spokesman said on Monday.
The warning was received last June by two intelligence specialists at the National Security Council, which advises the president on security issues, spokesman Mike McCurry said.
He told reporters it "dealt with allegations of Chinese attempts to funnel money to congressional candidates."

McCurry said those conducting the briefing asked that the information "not be disseminated or briefed higher up the chain of command here at the White House" and that the NSC officials "respected that admonishment."
"They were given a briefing on very specific ground rules and they honoured the ground rules," he said.

McCurry was responding to questions raised by a published report that the Federal Bureau of Investigation had warned the White House and six members of Congress of a Chinese plan to funnel money into last year's U.S. election campaign.
His disclosure added a bizarre new twist to a campaign financing controversy dogging Clinton and his Democratic Party, and one with potentially troubling and sensitive foreign policy implications.

It is illegal for foreign governments, citizens or business interests to contribute to U.S. political campaigns. Mounting evidence that such efforts took place raise questions as to whether the objective was to buy influence over U.S. foreign and trade policy decisions.
McCurry said he did not know why the FBI's concerns, which directly pertained to U.S. national security, were kept from Clinton and other policymakers.
"You're asking me to comment on the reasons why a briefer from the FBI requested that the information not be disseminated. I cannot explain that," he said.
When a reporter called it "appalling" the FBI would not tell Clinton of such a potentially serious matter, McCurry replied: "That's an idea that has not gone unnoticed."

The Washington Post reported on Sunday that China planned to spend nearly $2 million on covert campaign contributions, and that Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat, was among the lawmakers who had been warned about it. Feinstein has confirmed she received such a warning but said it was couched in vague and unhelpful terms.
Clinton's Democratic Party has returned nearly $3 million to donors -- most of them with links to Asian businesses or governments -- that were deemed questionable.
However, China reacted strongly to allegations it tried to meddle in U.S. politics, calling the charges unfounded and saying it had lodged a protest with the United States.
"The Chinese side has never got involved in U.S. political affairs in any form," the official Xinhua news agency quoted a senior Chinese foreign ministry official as saying.
Mei Ping, head of the Chinese foreign ministry's Americas department, said "slanderous news and reports about China" were damaging Chinese-American relations.
McCurry said that had the administration known about the alleged Chinese effort to curry favour with U.S. leaders it "might have acted diplomatically" to discourage this.
He said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had raised the issue with Chinese leaders during a recent Beijing visit.
Disclosure of the FBI suspicions came as pressure mounted on Attorney General Janet Reno to name an independent counsel to investigate the Democratic fund-raising controversy.
Congressional Republicans are already preparing to set up a Senate investigation. Various other committees in both houses of Congress are considering probes into various aspects of the issue.
